comment (2026-08-12) on ENT-1535 — then implement the floor-age circuit breaker
in go-nuts jsconsumer:

- Trigger: floor-stationary age > threshold (default 15–20 min, configurable).
  Measure floor-stationary time, NOT message stream-age.
- Action: dead-letter (raw msg + headers) then Ack. Never drop, never bare Term.
- Design constraint from the forensics: the library must own ONE retry mechanism.
  The NakWithDelay-vs-consumer-BackOff interaction (server stretches NAK delays
  by BackOff increments) made the configured ladder dead config — make that
  state unrepresentable (reject configs that set both, or wire them together).
- First adopter: entire-search search-indexer-refs (already on the post-#173
  ~43min ladder; the breaker replaces its retry-cap workaround).
- Acceptance (M1, Aug 22): synthetic poison event on repo_refs_v1 in staging
  dead-letters via the library path in ≤30 min; ack floor never pins >30 min;
  capture verified in repo_refs_dlq_v1 — note this is that DLQ's first real
  exercise; treat it as part of the test.

1	// Package jsconsumer is the durable JetStream pull-consumer scaffold shared by
2	// Entire's decode-and-dispatch consumers. Each of those used to hand-roll the
3	// same lifecycle: jetstream.New → CreateOrUpdateConsumer (durable, explicit
4	// ack, bounded ack-wait, bounded MaxDeliver, filter subject) → Consume → stop
5	// on context cancel; and the same per-message prologue: open a consumer span
6	// (re-parented across the NATS hop), decode the payload, and Term on a decode
7	// error.
8	//
9	// This package owns exactly that scaffold and nothing else. Each consumer
10	// keeps its OWN event type, business dispatch, metrics, and log lines — Start
11	// takes the consumer's message callback, and Process invokes the consumer's
12	// handle with the decoded event and the live span. The handler owns the
13	// message's terminal disposition (Ack/Nak/Term); Process never touches a
14	// message that decoded.
15	//

17	// module's shutdown classification ([nuts.IsShutdownFetchErr] gates the
18	// consume-error log so a drain during rollout isn't reported as a fault,

43		// when Config.AckWait is zero — comfortably longer than an RPC round-trip

52	// filter is given as either FilterSubject (single) or FilterSubjects (multi),
53	// mirroring jetstream.ConsumerConfig, so a migrated consumer preserves its
54	// existing on-server filter form exactly.
55	type Config struct {

57		Durable        string        // durable consumer name, stable across restarts
58		FilterSubject  string        // set this OR FilterSubjects
59		FilterSubjects []string      // set this OR FilterSubject
60		AckWait        time.Duration // 0 → DefaultAckWait (see EffectiveAckWait)
61		MaxDeliver     int           // 0 → DefaultMaxDeliver (see EffectiveMaxDeliver)

63		Name           string        // short consumer name, used as the log prefix
64	
65		// InactiveThreshold mirrors jetstream.ConsumerConfig.InactiveThreshold:

67		// server deletes it; zero means never (the JetStream default for
68		// durables). Consumers on interest-retention streams set this so a
69		// decommissioned durable stops pinning every message it would have
70		// received, instead of holding them until the stream's MaxAge.
71		InactiveThreshold time.Duration

82		Tracer trace.Tracer

113	// heartbeat by hand (a zero ackWait there is a no-op).

129	func (c Config) EffectiveMaxDeliver() int {

134	}

137	// [Start] (one-shot) and [Run] (supervised, which must fail fast on these
138	// rather than retry them forever).
139	func (c Config) validate(nc *nats.Conn, onMsg func(jetstream.Msg)) error {
140		if c.KeepInProgress && c.MaxMessages > 1 {
141			return fmt.Errorf("jsconsumer(%s): KeepInProgress requires MaxMessages <= 1: the heartbeat extends only the in-flight delivery, so %d buffered messages would exhaust AckWait behind a long handler", c.Name, c.MaxMessages)

198	// isShutdownConsumeErr reports whether a consume error is the benign result
199	// of the connection going away during shutdown. [nuts.IsShutdownFetchErr]
200	// covers the core nats.go sentinels, but the jetstream consume loop surfaces
201	// its OWN [jetstream.ErrConnectionClosed] — a distinct value that wraps
202	// neither — so it must be matched separately or a clean rollout drain still
203	// logs a warning (the COR-923 noise this suppression exists to remove). As
204	// with the root classifier, it is only "clean" when ctx is already done; a
205	// mid-run connection loss is a genuine fault worth logging.
206	func isShutdownConsumeErr(ctx context.Context, err error) bool {
207		return nuts.IsShutdownFetchErr(ctx, err) ||
208			(ctx.Err() != nil && errors.Is(err, jetstream.ErrConnectionClosed))
209	}

211	// Runner is a live consume loop. Stop halts it and is idempotent.
212	type Runner struct {
213		cc jetstream.ConsumeContext
214		// closed is cc.Closed(), captured while the subscription is live (the
215		// same channel is returned on every call, so capturing once avoids any
216		// post-Stop race) — it closes when the consume loop has fully wound
217		// down, including an in-flight handler.
218		closed <-chan struct{}
219		// watcherDone closes when Start's context-cancellation watcher exits. It is
220		// intentionally internal: callers synchronize on Stop, while tests pin that
221		// an explicit Stop does not retain a goroutine until the parent context ends.
222		watcherDone <-chan struct{}
223		stop        sync.Once
224	}

226	// Stop halts the consume loop and blocks until it has fully wound down —
227	// including an in-flight handler — so a caller may tear down what handlers
228	// use (stores, publishers, the NATS connection) the moment it returns: the
229	// cancel → join → drain shutdown ordering (COR-923). Safe on a nil or
230	// never-Started Runner, idempotent, and safe for concurrent use — an
231	// explicit Stop can race the context-cancel stop armed by Start. Must not be
232	// called from inside the handler; it would deadlock waiting on itself.
233	func (r *Runner) Stop() {
234		if r == nil || r.cc == nil {
235			return
236		}
237		r.stop.Do(r.cc.Stop)
238		<-r.closed
239	}

242	// messages to onMsg, returning a Runner that Stops when ctx is cancelled. The
243	// stream must already exist (provisioned declaratively); callers whose cells
244	// opt in per-stream gate Start behind that opt-in so a cell without the stream

246	//
247	// Consume errors are logged at Warn, except a drain/close during shutdown —
248	// both the core nats.go sentinels ([nuts.IsShutdownFetchErr]) and jetstream's

250	func Start(ctx context.Context, nc *nats.Conn, cfg Config, onMsg func(jetstream.Msg)) (*Runner, error) {
251		if err := cfg.validate(nc, onMsg); err != nil {
252			return nil, err
253		}
254		js, err := jetstream.New(nc)
255		if err != nil {
256			return nil, fmt.Errorf("jsconsumer(%s): jetstream.New: %w", cfg.Name, err)

260			AckPolicy:         jetstream.AckExplicitPolicy,
261			AckWait:           cfg.EffectiveAckWait(),

267		})

269			return nil, fmt.Errorf("jsconsumer(%s): create consumer %s/%s: %w", cfg.Name, cfg.Stream, cfg.Durable, err)

271		consumeOpts := []jetstream.PullConsumeOpt{jetstream.ConsumeErrHandler(func(_ jetstream.ConsumeContext, cerr error) {
272			if isShutdownConsumeErr(ctx, cerr) {
273				return
274			}

276		})}
277		switch {
278		case cfg.KeepInProgress:
279			consumeOpts = append(consumeOpts, jetstream.PullMaxMessages(1))
280		case cfg.MaxMessages > 0:
281			consumeOpts = append(consumeOpts, jetstream.PullMaxMessages(cfg.MaxMessages))
282		}

284		if err != nil {
285			return nil, fmt.Errorf("jsconsumer(%s): consume %s: %w", cfg.Name, cfg.Stream, err)

300	// isRetryableStartError classifies the narrow set of failures that can become
301	// healthy without changing Config or replacing nc. Everything else returns to
302	// the owner so a bad deployment cannot stay alive indefinitely with no
303	// consumer. Unknown server-side 5xx responses are retried, except known
304	// permanent JetStream configuration/account errors whose API happens to use a
305	// 5xx status.
306	func isRetryableStartError(err error) bool {
307		if errors.Is(err, jetstream.ErrStreamNotFound) ||
308			errors.Is(err, nats.ErrNoResponders) ||
309			errors.Is(err, nats.ErrTimeout) ||
310			errors.Is(err, nats.ErrDisconnected) {
311			return true
312		}
313	
314		var jsErr jetstream.JetStreamError
315		if !errors.As(err, &jsErr) || jsErr.APIError() == nil {
316			return false
317		}
318		apiErr := jsErr.APIError()
319		switch apiErr.ErrorCode { //nolint:exhaustive // unrecognized 5xx codes are deliberately retryable; all other unknown codes fail closed
320		case jetstream.JSErrCodeBadRequest,
321			jetstream.JSErrCodeConsumerCreate,
322			jetstream.JSErrCodeConsumerNameExists,
323			jetstream.JSErrCodeMaximumConsumersLimit,
324			jetstream.JSErrCodeJetStreamNotEnabledForAccount,
325			jetstream.JSErrCodeJetStreamNotEnabled,
326			jetstream.JSErrCodeConsumerAlreadyExists,
327			jetstream.JSErrCodeDuplicateFilterSubjects,
328			jetstream.JSErrCodeOverlappingFilterSubjects,
329			jetstream.JSErrCodeConsumerEmptyFilter,
330			jetstream.JSErrCodeConsumerExists:
331			return false
332		default:
333			return apiErr.Code >= 500
334		}
335	}

337	// Retry envelope for [Run]'s supervision: exponential from runRetryInitial
338	// doubling to runRetryMax, reset once a consume loop survives longer than the
339	// max. Package vars (not consts) so tests can compress the schedule.
340	var (
341		runRetryInitial = time.Second
342		runRetryMax     = 30 * time.Second
343	)
344	
345	// Run supervises the consume loop [Start] builds. Where Start is one-shot —
346	// an error at consumer creation is returned, and a consume loop that closes
347	// underneath the caller (consumer deleted on the server, subscription
348	// invalidated) stays closed — Run retries both with exponential backoff
349	// (runRetryInitial doubling to runRetryMax, reset after a loop that outlives
350	// the max). In particular a stream that is not provisioned yet at boot — the
351	// declarative-provisioning race — is a retry, not a crash.
352	//
353	// Run blocks until ctx is cancelled, then joins the live loop (including an
354	// in-flight handler, see [Runner.Stop]) before returning, so it composes with
355	// the cancel → join → drain shutdown ordering as the body of a supervised
356	// goroutine:
357	//
358	//	g.Go(func(ctx context.Context) {
359	//		if err := jsconsumer.Run(ctx, nc, cfg, onMsg); err != nil {
360	//			log.Error("consumer config rejected", "error", err)
361	//		}
362	//	})
363	//
364	// Local configuration errors and permanent server responses (invalid consumer
365	// configuration, authorization/account setup) can never succeed on retry and
366	// are returned immediately. A missing declarative stream, temporary transport
367	// failure, or unknown server-side 5xx response remains supervised. A nil return
368	// means a clean, ctx-driven exit.
369	func Run(ctx context.Context, nc *nats.Conn, cfg Config, onMsg func(jetstream.Msg)) error {
370		if err := cfg.validate(nc, onMsg); err != nil {
371			return err
372		}
373		delay := runRetryInitial
374		for {
375			// Each attempt gets a child context so the cancel-watcher goroutine
376			// Start arms is released when the attempt dies, instead of one
377			// accumulating per recreate for the life of the process.
378			attemptCtx, cancelAttempt := context.WithCancel(ctx)
379			r, err := Start(attemptCtx, nc, cfg, onMsg)
380			if err != nil {
381				cancelAttempt()
382				if ctx.Err() != nil {
383					return nil //nolint:nilerr // a Start error during shutdown is a clean, ctx-driven exit, not a fault to report
384				}
385				if !isRetryableStartError(err) {
386					return err
387				}
388				cfg.logger().WarnContext(ctx, cfg.Name+": start consumer failed; retrying",
389					slog.Any("error", err), slog.Duration("retry_in", delay))
390			} else {
391				started := time.Now()
392				select {
393				case <-ctx.Done():
394					r.Stop()
395					cancelAttempt()
396					return nil
397				case <-r.closed:
398					cancelAttempt()
399					if ctx.Err() != nil {
400						return nil //nolint:nilerr // the loop closing during shutdown is the expected wind-down, not a fault
401					}
402					// A loop that ran long enough to be called healthy earns a
403					// fresh envelope; a flapping one keeps escalating.
404					if time.Since(started) >= runRetryMax {
405						delay = runRetryInitial
406					}
407					cfg.logger().WarnContext(ctx, cfg.Name+": consume loop closed; recreating",
408						slog.Duration("retry_in", delay))
409				}
410			}
411			select {
412			case <-ctx.Done():

13	// delay envelope without a message in hand.
14	//
15	// # Zero-value and unlimited semantics
16	//

42	package backoff
43	
44	import (
45		"fmt"
46		"math"
47		"time"
48	
49		"github.com/nats-io/nats.go/jetstream"
50	)
51	
52	// UnlimitedMaxDeliver is the explicit Policy.MaxDeliver value for unlimited
53	// redeliveries (matching jetstream.ConsumerConfig.MaxDeliver, where a
54	// non-positive value disables the delivery cap). The zero value means the same
55	// thing; the named constant lets a caller say so on purpose.
56	const UnlimitedMaxDeliver = -1
57	
58	// Outcome is the disposition NakOrTerm chose, for the caller's metrics and
59	// logs.
60	type Outcome string
61	
62	const (
63		OutcomeNak  Outcome = "nak"
64		OutcomeTerm Outcome = "term"
65	)
66	
67	// Policy is the redelivery envelope a consumer applies to transient
68	// failures. MaxDeliver must match the consumer's on-server MaxDeliver — the
69	// policy detects the final delivery by comparing against it.
70	type Policy struct {
71		// NakDelay is the base delay before redelivery, and with a zero Factor
72		// the whole envelope: flat suits failures expected to clear on their own
73		// timetable, with MaxDeliver bounding the total.
74		NakDelay time.Duration
75		// Factor is the optional multiplicative growth per prior delivery: the
76		// Nth delivery naks with NakDelay × Factor^(N-1), capped at MaxDelay.
77		// Values ≤ 1 (including the zero value) keep the flat envelope. Growing
78		// envelopes suit failures that get cheaper to wait out than to retry —
79		// a downstream in a crash loop, a rate limit — where hammering on the
80		// flat cadence spends MaxDeliver too fast.
81		Factor float64
82		// MaxDelay caps the grown delay; it does nothing for a flat policy.
83		// Zero with a growing Factor leaves growth bounded only by MaxDeliver
84		// ending the redeliveries (the computed delay still saturates rather
85		// than overflowing).
86		MaxDelay time.Duration
87		// MaxDeliver is the consumer's redelivery cap
88		// (jetstream.ConsumerConfig.MaxDeliver). Non-positive (0 or
89		// UnlimitedMaxDeliver) means unlimited redeliveries — matching the
90		// jetstream field's semantics — so no delivery is ever final and NakOrTerm
91		// always Naks.
92		MaxDeliver int
93		// TermOnExhaustion makes the final delivery Term instead of Nak, so a
94		// work-queue message is removed cleanly rather than orphaning un-acked
95		// (COR-762). Callers with a DLQ capture before calling NakOrTerm.
96		TermOnExhaustion bool
97	}
98	
99	// NakOrTerm applies the policy to a transiently-failed [jetstream.Msg]
100	// delivery: NakWithDelay (see [Policy.DelayFor]) for redelivery, or — on the
101	// final delivery with TermOnExhaustion set — Term. Without TermOnExhaustion the
102	// final delivery still Naks; the broker drops the Nak at MaxDeliver and the
103	// stream's retention decides the message's fate.
104	//
105	// The returned Outcome reports which disposition was chosen, for the caller's
106	// metrics and logs. A disposition error is worth a log line but nothing more:
107	// a failed Nak redelivers via AckWait expiry anyway, and a failed Term on a
108	// work-queue stream means the message lingers exactly as it would have without
109	// the policy.
110	func (p Policy) NakOrTerm(msg jetstream.Msg) (Outcome, error) {
111		if p.TermOnExhaustion && IsFinalDelivery(msg, p.MaxDeliver) {
112			if err := msg.Term(); err != nil {
113				return OutcomeTerm, fmt.Errorf("term on final delivery: %w", err)
114			}
115			return OutcomeTerm, nil
116		}
117		if err := msg.NakWithDelay(p.DelayFor(NumDelivered(msg))); err != nil {
118			return OutcomeNak, fmt.Errorf("nak with delay: %w", err)
119		}
120		return OutcomeNak, nil
121	}
122	
123	// DelayFor reports the redelivery delay the policy applies after delivery
124	// number numDelivered (1 on first delivery): NakDelay for a flat policy,
125	// NakDelay × Factor^(numDelivered-1) capped at MaxDelay for a growing one.
126	// numDelivered ≤ 1 — including the 0 that [NumDelivered] reports when
127	// metadata is unavailable — reads as the first delivery. Exposed so a caller
128	// can log or meter the delay it is about to apply.
129	func (p Policy) DelayFor(numDelivered int) time.Duration {
130		if p.Factor <= 1 || numDelivered <= 1 {
131			return p.NakDelay
132		}
133		d := float64(p.NakDelay) * math.Pow(p.Factor, float64(numDelivered-1))
134		if p.MaxDelay > 0 && d >= float64(p.MaxDelay) {
135			return p.MaxDelay
136		}
137		if d >= float64(math.MaxInt64) {
138			// Uncapped growth outran time.Duration; saturate instead of wrapping
139			// negative (a negative NakWithDelay would redeliver immediately).
140			return math.MaxInt64
141		}
142		return time.Duration(d)
143	}
144	
145	// NumDelivered reports the JetStream delivery count of a [jetstream.Msg]
146	// (1 on first delivery), or 0 if metadata is unavailable (e.g. a synthetic test
147	// message).
148	func NumDelivered(msg jetstream.Msg) int {
149		if meta, err := msg.Metadata(); err == nil && meta != nil {
150			return int(meta.NumDelivered)
151		}
152		return 0
153	}
154	
155	// IsFinalDelivery reports whether this is the last delivery before JetStream
156	// stops redelivering (NumDelivered has reached MaxDeliver), so a transient
157	// failure here is terminal rather than another Nak-and-retry. A non-positive
158	// maxDeliver means unlimited redeliveries (the jetstream.ConsumerConfig
159	// semantics), so no delivery is final — without the guard the zero value
160	// would read every delivery as final and Term on the first failure.
161	// Unavailable metadata also reads as non-final: the safe default is another
162	// retry, not a Term.
163	func IsFinalDelivery(msg jetstream.Msg, maxDeliver int) bool {
164		if maxDeliver <= 0 {
165			return false
166		}
167		if meta, err := msg.Metadata(); err == nil && meta != nil {
168			return meta.NumDelivered >= uint64(maxDeliver)
169		}
170		return false
171	}

13	// dlqPublishTimeout bounds one dead-letter PublishMsg. The consume context has
14	// no deadline, and PublishMsg waits for the PubAck indefinitely; without a
15	// bound a NATS blip would hang the handler (and, since a one-in-flight consumer
16	// keeps a slot occupied, stall the consumer) instead of failing the capture
17	// loudly.
18	const dlqPublishTimeout = 15 * time.Second
19	
20	// DLQ provenance headers added to the captured copy so a replay tool (or a
21	// human) can see why and from where a message was dead-lettered.
22	const (
23		DLQReasonHeader    = "Nats-Dlq-Reason"
24		DLQOriginHeader    = "Nats-Dlq-Origin-Subject"
25		DLQDeliveredHeader = "Nats-Dlq-Delivered"
26		DLQStreamSeqHeader = "Nats-Dlq-Stream-Seq"
27	)
28	
29	// DLQPublisher is the publish surface DeadLetter needs — the modern
30	// [JetStream] publish primitive (satisfied by jetstream.JetStream), aliased
31	// so DeadLetter's signature reads in DLQ terms. Kept minimal so wiring can
32	// hand it the same JetStream handle the per-cell publishers already hold,
33	// and tests can stub it.
34	type DLQPublisher = JetStream
35	
36	// SubjectToken sanitizes s into a single valid NATS subject token. NATS tokens
37	// cannot contain spaces, dots, or wildcards, so every character outside
38	// [a-z0-9_-] is replaced with '_' (and letters are lowercased). Use it to turn a
39	// human-readable dead-letter reason ("bad completion payload") into a subject
40	// token ("bad_completion_payload") — publishing to an unsanitized reason would
41	// fail, so the caller would never Ack the poison off a WorkQueue.
42	func SubjectToken(s string) string {
43		// Iterate bytes, not runes: we only keep ASCII [a-z0-9_-] and map everything
44		// else (including every byte of a multi-byte rune) to '_', so a byte loop is
45		// both correct and free of a rune->byte narrowing conversion.
46		b := make([]byte, 0, len(s))
47		for i := range len(s) {
48			c := s[i]
49			switch {
50			case c >= 'a' && c <= 'z', c >= '0' && c <= '9', c == '_', c == '-':
51				b = append(b, c)
52			case c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z':
53				b = append(b, c-'A'+'a')
54			default:
55				b = append(b, '_')
56			}
57		}
58		if len(b) == 0 {
59			return "unknown"
60		}
61		return string(b)
62	}
63	
64	// DeadLetter republishes a poison message to dlqSubject, preserving its payload
65	// and headers and adding Nats-Dlq-* provenance (reason, origin subject,
66	// delivery count, stream sequence).
67	//
68	// It is the capture step a consumer runs before giving up on a message it can
69	// never process. DeadLetter copies the poison to a durable DLQ subject so it can
70	// be inspected or replayed, and the caller then removes the original from the
71	// stream — a Term on the final delivery (see backoff.Policy.TermOnExhaustion,
72	// whose doc notes callers "DLQ capture before calling NakOrTerm") or a plain
73	// Ack. Without this step a Term'd or MaxDeliver-exhausted message is discarded
74	// with no trail; DeadLetter is what makes the give-up auditable and recoverable.
75	//
76	// Returns an error if the republish fails; on error the caller MUST NOT remove
77	// the original — Nak or leave it so the poison is never dropped without a
78	// captured copy. Publishing is bounded by dlqPublishTimeout regardless of ctx's
79	// deadline.
80	func DeadLetter(ctx context.Context, pub DLQPublisher, dlqSubject string, msg jetstream.Msg, reason string) error {
81		hdr := nats.Header{}
82		for k, v := range msg.Headers() {
83			hdr[k] = append([]string(nil), v...)
84		}
85		hdr.Set(DLQReasonHeader, reason)
86		hdr.Set(DLQOriginHeader, msg.Subject())
87		if meta, err := msg.Metadata(); err == nil && meta != nil {
88			hdr.Set(DLQDeliveredHeader, strconv.FormatUint(meta.NumDelivered, 10))
89			hdr.Set(DLQStreamSeqHeader, strconv.FormatUint(meta.Sequence.Stream, 10))
90		}
91	
92		out := &nats.Msg{Subject: dlqSubject, Data: msg.Data(), Header: hdr}
93	
94		pubCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, dlqPublishTimeout)
95		defer cancel()
96		if _, err := pub.PublishMsg(pubCtx, out); err != nil {
97			return fmt.Errorf("dead-letter publish to %q: %w", dlqSubject, err)
98		}
99		return nil
100	}

# go-nuts A small, dependency-light toolkit over [`nats.go`](https://github.com/nats-io/nats.go) for building [NATS](https://nats.io) and JetStream services in Go. The root package handles connection lifecycle — connecting, draining, and shutting down cleanly; opt-in subpackages add a durable JetStream pull-consumer scaffold, a publish helper, trace-context propagation, and a redelivery policy. ## Install ``` go get github.com/entireio/go-nuts ``` ## Connection lifecycle (root package) - **`Connect`** — dial with a resilient default posture: reconnect-forever (so a long-lived service rides out a NATS outage instead of permanently closing after the client's default 60 attempts), a bounded drain timeout, optional rotation-aware mTLS, and lifecycle log handlers that don't mistake a clean shutdown for a fault. Async errors (slow-consumer drops, permissions violations) and lame-duck notices are logged through the configured logger instead of nats.go's stderr default. - **`Drain` / `IsShutdownFetchErr`** — graceful shutdown. `Drain` starts nats.go's asynchronous drain and blocks until the connection flushes and closes (bounded by a timeout), returning an error and force-closing when it cannot complete; `IsShutdownFetchErr` lets a fetch loop treat a drain/close during shutdown as a clean exit rather than an error. - **`ShutdownGroup`** — cancels tracked background loops, waits for them to return, then drains the registered connections — the ordering that keeps a `Drain` from racing an in-flight `Fetch`. A panic or unexpected return in a tracked loop cancels the group and is returned by `Shutdown`, so a dead consumer cannot leave its process looking healthy. ## Usage The example below drives a hand-rolled fetch loop on nats.go's legacy pull API; consumers on the modern `jetstream` API get the whole loop from [`jsconsumer`](#subpackages) instead. ```go ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM) defer stop() g := nuts.NewShutdownGroup(ctx) nc, err := nuts.Connect(g.Context(), natsURL, nuts.WithName("worker")) if err != nil { return err } g.AddConn("worker", nc) g.Go(func(ctx context.Context) { for { // Stop fetching once the group is shutting down, so the loop returns // before its connection is drained (Shutdown cancels, joins, then // drains — the loop must observe the cancel to keep that ordering). if ctx.Err() != nil { return } msgs, err := sub.Fetch(1, nats.MaxWait(5*time.Second)) switch { case errors.Is(err, nats.ErrTimeout): continue // idle poll case nuts.IsShutdownFetchErr(ctx, err): return // clean shutdown: connection drained/closed case err != nil: // Real error — log/metric, then back off so a fast-failing Fetch // (e.g. connection closed mid-run) does not busy-spin the CPU. slog.ErrorContext(ctx, "fetch failed", slog.Any("error", err)) select { case <-ctx.Done(): case <-time.After(time.Second): } continue } handle(msgs) } }) <-g.Context().Done() // process signal, or a tracked loop failed if err := g.Shutdown(); err != nil { // cancel loops → join → drain, in that order return err } ``` By default `Connect` builds mTLS from the `ENTIRE_INTERNAL_TLS_{CERT,KEY,CA}_FILE` environment variables; use `WithTLSConfig`, `WithoutTLS`, or the other `Option`s to override. ## Subpackages The root package is deliberately nats.go-only. The consumer-side layers live in subpackages so importing the root links none of their dependencies (`natsmsg` and `jsconsumer` add the OpenTelemetry API; all three use `nats.go/jetstream`): - **`natsmsg`** — small JetStream message helpers: W3C trace-context propagation over message headers (`Inject` / `ExtractHeader` / `StartConsumerSpan`, so publish → consume stitches into one trace), `Publisher` — the publish core (producer span with a caller-selected `Operation` name + standard `messaging.*` attributes + trace inject + `Nats-Msg-Id` dedup + bounded pub-ack wait + PubAck telemetry, with `StartProducerSpan` for callers composing by hand); it owns just that prologue — subject construction, payload encoding, domain metrics/logging, and the response to a failed publish stay with the caller (its `JS` field is the narrow publish slice of `jetstream.JetStream`, so tests stub one method). Also `KeepInProgress`, an AckWait heartbeat for long handlers, capped so a wedged handler still redelivers, and `DeadLetter` / `SubjectToken`, the dead-letter capture that copies a poison message to a DLQ subject with `Nats-Dlq-*` provenance before a consumer gives up on it (the capture step `backoff`'s Term-on-exhaustion below expects). `natsmsg/natsmsgtest` ships `FakeMsg`, a scriptable message for asserting a consumer's ack/nak/term disposition without a broker. - **`jsconsumer`** — the durable JetStream pull-consumer scaffold: `Start` (create-or-update durable → consume → stop on context cancel), `Run` (`Start` under supervision: recreate on a closed loop with exponential backoff, tolerate a not-yet-provisioned stream at boot), and `Process` (consumer span re-parented across the NATS hop → decode → Term-on-undecodable → dispatch to the handler, which owns the message's disposition). AckExplicit, bounded AckWait and MaxDeliver, optional InactiveThreshold / MaxAckPending, shutdown-aware consume-error logging, optional `KeepInProgress` heartbeat. - **`backoff`** — the redelivery policy for transiently-failed deliveries: a `NakWithDelay` envelope — flat by default, optionally growing per delivery (`Factor`/`MaxDelay`) — bounded by MaxDeliver, with opt-in Term-on-final-delivery so a work-queue message is removed cleanly instead of orphaning un-acked. It owns disposition and delay calculation only (`NakOrTerm` over `jetstream.Msg`). MaxDeliver mirrors `jetstream.ConsumerConfig`: a non-positive value (`0` or `UnlimitedMaxDeliver`) means unlimited redeliveries, so bridge an unset `jsconsumer` consumer with its `EffectiveMaxDeliver()` rather than the raw field. ## Development Requires Go 1.26. Tasks via [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev): `mise run test`, `mise run lint`, `mise run fmt`. ## License MIT — see [LICENSE](./LICENSE).

The floor-age circuit breaker is implemented in `jsconsumer`, tests and lint green (`go test -race ./...`, `golangci-lint run`: 0 issues). I did not commit — say the word and I will.

## What landed

**`jsconsumer/retry.go`** — `Retry`, the consumer's single retry mechanism: one ladder, the breaker, and the dead-letter capture both terminate into.

- **Trigger is floor-stationary age**, read from the durable's real `AckFloor.Stream` by a poll `Start` runs and `Stop` joins — not message stream-age, per the forensics' 35-min receipt→first-delivery lag finding. Default `FloorAge` 15m, `FloorPoll` derives to 30s. Age is measured from *first observation* of a floor value, so a fresh process under-reports an old stall: the breaker can be late, never early.
- **Action is dead-letter-then-Ack.** `Settle` picks exactly one of breaker / exhaustion / ladder. `TermOnExhaustion: true` is a construction error, and a `Term` never happens on any path (pinned by `TestSettleNeverTerms`). A failed DLQ publish Naks instead of dropping and returns `settle:dlq_publish_failed`, leaving the floor pinned so the monitor fires — ENT-1492's deliberate posture.
- **Blocker predicate is `stream_seq == floor+1`** — the same identification the runbook makes by hand, and exactly the incident's 2,774,436/2,774,437 pair. Deliberately *not* "any sequence above the floor": that would take a merely-slow event away from a ladder it might still recover on (the eu-west-1 attempt-4 recovery). Guarded further by `MinDeliveries` (default 2), so a message is never dead-lettered on the delivery that first failed.

**One retry mechanism, enforced.** `Config.BackOff` (server ladder) and `Config.Retry` are mutually exclusive — a `Start` error, not a warning. `Retry.MaxDeliver` is cross-checked against `EffectiveMaxDeliver()`. And a rung longer than `FloorAge` is rejected, because the breaker only acts on a delivery: that's the same "configured ladder isn't the real envelope" disease one level up. Critically, `Start` always sends `BackOff` — nil under a `Retry` — so adopting the library **clears the stale six-rung ladder already on the durable**. `TestStartClearsStaleServerBackOff` verifies that against a real embedded server; without it, adoption would leave the two schedulers composing exactly as ENT-1535 found them.

**Beyond the ask, flagging it:** `Process` now dead-letters an undecodable payload instead of a bare `Term` when a `Retry` is configured (unchanged without one). That was the last drop-without-a-record surface in the scaffold, and "never drop, never bare Term" applies to it identically — but it is adjacent to ENT-1496, which ENT-1601 scopes separately.

## For M1 (Aug 22)

Recommended `search-indexer-refs` config is in the `Retry` doc comment: flat 5m rung, `MaxDeliver` 5, `FloorAge` 15m → **worst-case pin 15m + 5m + 30s = 20m30s**, inside the ≤30 min SLA with headroom.

**One thing to confirm during the staging exercise.** `repo_refs_v1` is a single `repo_refs_v1.>` wildcard over 29 subjects with 5 consumers, but I could not read `search-indexer-refs`'s own filter subject from the MCP surface. If that filter is narrower than the stream, stream-sequence gaps could put the blocker somewhere other than `floor+1` and the breaker would never identify it. The incident data says otherwise (blocker sat one sequence above the floor), so I kept the exact predicate — but I made the failure loud rather than silent: `ack floor stalled but no delivery at floor+1` logs the sequence it wanted against the one it saw, once per stationary period. If the synthetic poison event dead-letters, the predicate holds; if that line appears instead, it tells you precisely why. Worth watching for alongside the `repo_refs_dlq_v1` capture check, since this is that DLQ's first real exercise.

1. [P1] Idle time incorrectly ages newly arrived work — jsconsumer/retry.go:419

     The poll starts the stationary timer even when NumAckPending == 0. After a healthy consumer sits idle for 16 minutes, the next message at floor+1 is dead-lettered on its second attempt as though it had stalled for 16 minutes. This
     also makes FloorStationaryFor and the warning log report healthy idle consumers as stalled.

  2. [P1] The breaker cannot identify blockers for filtered consumers — jsconsumer/retry.go:476

     Matching meta.Sequence.Stream == ackFloor.Stream+1 assumes stream sequences are dense. Filters make them sparse. JetStream provides consumer sequences specifically for this: compare meta.Sequence.Consumer with AckFloor.Consumer+1. A
     reproduced floor at stream 100/consumer 1 followed by stream 200/consumer 2 remained on the retry ladder indefinitely instead of tripping the breaker.

  3. [P1] Failed final DLQ capture is reported as retried, but no retry occurs — jsconsumer/retry.go:553

     On the final delivery, a failed capture calls NakWithDelay and returns OutcomeRetried. MaxDeliver has already been reached, so NATS retires the delivery instead. Against the pinned NATS server, MaxDeliver: 2 produced exactly two
     deliveries, then ack_pending=0; no third capture attempt occurred. The original remains uncaptured and requires manual recovery. DeadLetter has the same fallback at line 598.

  What I would keep:

The reviewer found two real bugs. Let me evaluate each claim against what I built.

**Where they're right, and it matters:**

1. **Idle-consumer false positive — genuine bug.** My stall clock runs on floor-stationarity alone. On a quiet consumer the floor sits still because *nothing arrived*, not because anything is stuck. A new message then arrives at `floor+1`, hits one transient failure, and gets dead-lettered on attempt 2 with a "4-hour stall" behind it. That converts the breaker from a poison remedy into "one retry then DLQ." My tests didn't catch it because they all arm the floor with a blocker already present.

2. **`OutcomeRetried` on terminal capture failure is a lie — genuine bug.** At delivery 5 of 5, a failed DLQ publish gets a Nak the broker drops. Nothing retries it. Reporting `retried` tells the adopter's metrics the opposite of the truth.

Fixing both now, since they hold under either architecture.

The breaker triggers on **floor-stall age**, not message stream-age: the two
  diverge badly under backlog, where 35 minutes of receipt→first-delivery lag
  on a perfectly healthy message would read as a stall. Stalled is also not the
  same as *stationary* — the clock runs only while the consumer has delivered

  `Stop`; `FloorStall` exposes the stall for the adopter's own gauge.

  Never a drop, and never a bare `Term`. A failed capture Naks instead, so the
  message survives and the stall stays visible — and `CaptureReserve` holds
  back deliveries specifically to retry it. When even those are spent the
  message is reported as `OutcomeStranded`, not dressed up as a retry: a Nak
  at the broker's cap is dropped, so nothing will touch it again and it needs
  the break-glass runbook. Alert on that outcome.

  fate, so it ships with `BreakerObserveOnly`: evaluate and report the trip,

package jsconsumer // import "github.com/entireio/go-nuts/jsconsumer"

Package jsconsumer is the durable JetStream pull-consumer scaffold shared by
Entire's decode-and-dispatch consumers. Each of those used to hand-roll the
same lifecycle: jetstream.New → CreateOrUpdateConsumer (durable, explicit ack,
bounded ack-wait, bounded MaxDeliver, filter subject) → Consume → stop on
context cancel; and the same per-message prologue: open a consumer span
(re-parented across the NATS hop), decode the payload, and Term on a decode
error.

This package owns exactly that scaffold and nothing else. Each consumer keeps
its OWN event type, business dispatch, metrics, and log lines — Start takes the
consumer's message callback, and Process invokes the consumer's handle with
the decoded event and the live span. The handler owns the message's terminal
disposition (Ack/Nak/Term); Process never touches a message that decoded.

The one exception to "disposition stays with the handler" is Retry,
the scaffold's optional single retry mechanism: the redelivery ladder and the
dead-letter capture it terminates into (ENT-1535). A handler that configures
one calls Retry.Settle instead of picking a disposition itself, and the package
guarantees the consumer has exactly one redelivery scheduler — a server-side
Config.BackOff and a Retry are mutually exclusive, because together neither is
the real envelope.

FloorMonitor is the separate, advisory half: it polls the durable's ack floor
and reports how long it has been stalled. Hand it to a Retry and it becomes the
floor-age circuit breaker, dead-lettering the message pinning a stalled floor;
use it alone and it is just the health signal, leaving the quarantine decision
to the adopter.

**Two findings I accepted as bugs and fixed:**

*Idle-consumer false positive.* My stall clock ran on floor-stationarity alone. *`OutcomeRetried` was a lie at the cap.* A failed capture on the broker's final delivery gets a Nak the broker drops; nothing retries. ## Finding 1 (P1) — real, but the prescribed fix is also broken

I probed both predicates against a live server before changing anything. Two scenarios, and they disagree:

| | blocker still pending when its predecessor acked | after a full drain, gap before the blocker |
|---|---|---|
| `AckFloor.Stream+1` | matches on **every** delivery | **fails** (floor 2, blocker at stream 6) |
| `AckFloor.Consumer+1` | matches on delivery 1, then **2/4, 3/5, 4/6 — all fail** | **fails** |

You're right that mine breaks for filtered consumers. But `AckFloor.Consumer` is not the fix: the server only recomputes that floor when the message *at* the floor is acked, so it pins to the blocker's **first** delivery and goes stale the instant it's redelivered. With `MinDeliveries ≥ 2` — the default, and the guard that stops us dead-lettering a message on its first failure — it would never match. Switching would have disabled the breaker outright while looking like a fix.

So I stopped trying to identify the blocker; consumer info doesn't carry that. `shouldQuarantine` now requires three independently-true facts: the monitor reports the floor stalled past `FloorAge`; this message's stream sequence is above the floor (exact, gap-proof); and this message has *itself* been failing at least `FloorAge`, computed from its delivery count against the ladder. Gap-proof, redelivery-proof, multi-replica-safe, and it's the forensics' own "dead-letter instead of NAK when scheduling attempt 4." `TestBreakerIsIndependentOfTheGapToTheFloor` runs floor+1, +2, +164, +100000.

Cost, stated plainly: during a stall this may quarantine a message that was failing *alongside* the blocker rather than being it. It goes to the DLQ with full provenance and is replayable. That residual is in the type doc.

## Finding 2 (P2) — fixed, and the underlying weakness with it

Now `DoubleAck` with a bounded context, not fire-and-forget `Ack`: a lost plain Ack would leave the floor pinned with nothing reporting it. Classification is now three-way — `Captured` distinguishes "data safe, original stuck" from "nothing preserved". At the cap, capture-then-failed-ack reports `OutcomeStranded`, not `OutcomeRetried`.

## Finding 3 (P2) — fix applied, but I could not reproduce it

I added the join and then tried to make it fail without one: instrumented `FloorMonitor` with a concurrent-poll high-water mark, forced repeated close-and-recreate cycles at 1ms polling under `-race -count=3`. **Clean with and without the fix.** `cancelAttempt()` already cancels the poll's context — including the in-flight `Info` — and the recreate sits behind the retry delay (1s in production, 20ms compressed), so the window is microseconds against that.

I kept the join anyway: `Runner.Stop`'s contract is "wound down, safe to tear down what it uses", and `Run` bypassing it made that timing-dependent rather than unconditional. But I'm not claiming a regression test — `TestRunJoinsThePollBeforeRecreating` asserts the invariant and would catch a future refactor that drops the join *and* shortens the delay; it does not discriminate today. If your probe hit it deterministically I'd like to see how.

## Rollout — taken

`BreakerObserveOnly bool` → `Breaker BreakerMode`, zero value `BreakerObserve`. Handing a `Retry` a monitor now buys the measurement and nothing else; `BreakerEnforce` is an affirmative opt-in. search-indexer-refs sets it explicitly for M1, per your earlier call.

One config consequence worth flagging: with the ladder now carrying the message-local half of the trigger, `MaxDeliver 5` put the breaker and ladder exhaustion on the same delivery. The documented adopter config is `MaxDeliver 6` / flat 5m — breaker eligible at delivery 4 (15m), ladder spent at 5, sixth reserved for a failed capture. Worst-case pin unchanged at 20m30s.

Settle is the only entry point to the library's dispositions, so such a message is not settled by any of them — ladder, exhaustion or breaker. jsconsumer: one retry schedule, dead-letter capture, and floor telemetry

ENT-1535's stall had two causes, and only one of them was the poison message.
search-indexer-refs advertised a 5m/10m/30m/1h/4h/12h ladder while the
forensics measured a real 34h22m envelope: the handler's NakWithDelay and the
consumer's BackOff were both scheduling redelivery, so the server stretched
each NAK by the BackOff increments and neither ladder was the truth. A
configured schedule that lies is how a single unindexable ref event pinned an
ack floor for ~10h with nothing in the system saying why.

So this makes the schedule singular and checkable, and gives a consumer a
non-lossy way to give up.

  Schedule       the retry timing as plain values, and the ONE implementation
                 of the arithmetic that says whether it hangs together. Pure —
                 no connection, no I/O, no clock — so the same function runs at
                 Start, in fleet CI's admission lint over a rendered Consumer
                 CR, and (later) at bind time against the durable's live
                 config. Duplicated timing maths is how ENT-1535 happened;
                 compile this in rather than restating it.
  Retry          where retries END: dead-letter capture, then settle. The
                 SERVER owns when they happen, through the durable's BackOff;
                 Retry plain-Naks into it and has no ladder fields at all, so
                 two competing schedulers are unrepresentable rather than
                 merely rejected.
  FloorMonitor   the ack-floor stall signal, as telemetry. Separate from
                 disposition because ack-floor state is consumer-global while
                 giving up on a message is message-local.

Never a drop and never a bare Term (ENT-1492): a failed capture Naks instead,
CaptureReserve holds deliveries back to retry it, and when even those are spent
the settlement reports OutcomeStranded rather than dressing it up as a retry —
a Nak at the broker's cap is dropped, so nothing will touch that message again.
The terminal Ack is a bounded DoubleAck, because a lost fire-and-forget Ack
leaves the floor pinned with nothing reporting it.

The floor-age circuit breaker is here, wired to FloorMonitor, and is
EXPERIMENTAL. BreakerObserve is the zero value and the only supported mode:
it measures what enforcing would do, spending the same one-per-stall-window
budget so the counts are a faithful dry run. Every serious defect found in
review was in the enforce path, all from one root — acting on a client-side
inference about which message holds a consumer-global floor. Deleting it is an
acceptable outcome of the soak if bounded ladders prove sufficient.

Notable behaviours worth knowing about:

  - Stall age is measured while the consumer has delivered PAST its own floor.
    An idle consumer's motionless floor is not a stall, and charging the next
    arriving message with that idle time would quarantine it on delivery two.
  - Elapsed failure time is measured, not inferred from NumDelivered, which
    JetStream also increments on AckWait expiry — a panicking handler can burn
    four deliveries in milliseconds.
  - Schedule.TimeToDeadLetter repeats the last backOff rung once the array runs
    out, as the server does. A short array under a larger maxDeliver is not a
    short ladder, and under-counting would pass a config that breaches its
    bound in production.
  - Process dead-letters an undecodable payload instead of Terming it when a
    Retry is configured, closing the last drop-without-a-record surface.

Explicit non-goal: a handler that DIES on the poison message rather than
returning an error. Settle is the only entry point to every disposition here,
so such a message is not settled by any of them — a property of the callback
contract, not of the breaker. Recovering the panic to Ack it would hide the bug
and leave handler state unreconciled, against ShutdownGroup's existing
fatal-panic posture. Detection is unaffected; remediation is not attempted.

Refs ENT-1601, ENT-1535, ENT-1492, COR-762.
